paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. Good madam, let me see your face.

units.o: Good madam, let me see your face.
units.m: Good madam, let me see your face.

reasons: keep: already plain modern English.

paragraphs.speaker: OLIVIA.
paragraphs.proposed: OLIVIA. Do you have any commission from your lord to negotiate with my face? Now you've strayed from your text. But we will draw the curtain and show you the picture. [Unveiling.] Look, sir: a portrait of me as I was just this moment. Isn't it well done?

units.o: Have you any commission from your lord to negotiate with my face?
units.m: Do you have any commission from your lord to negotiate with my face?

units.o: You are now out of your text:
units.m: Now you've strayed from your text.

units.o: but we will draw the curtain and show you the picture.
units.m: But we will draw the curtain and show you the picture.

units.o: [_Unveiling._]
units.m: [Unveiling.]

units.o: Look you, sir, such a one I was this present.
units.m: Look, sir: a portrait of me as I was just this moment.

units.o: Is’t not well done?
units.m: Isn't it well done?

reasons: Unnatural syntax fixed and joke restored: 'such a one I was this present' = 'this is how I looked at this very moment' (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, present subst. 2: 'such a one I was this p.', Tw. I,5,253, '== this moment'; Onions 1911, present sb. 2: 'adv. (?) = just now', same line). Olivia labels her unveiled face like a dated portrait inscription, continuing 'draw the curtain and show you the picture'. Current 'Look, sir, just like this I was at this present time' keeps the inverted order, and the listener cannot hear the portrait joke.

Unidiomatic phrase fixed: 'out of your text' continues the sermon joke ('what is your text?', 'chapter', 'heresy'; Onions 1911, text 2 'quotation, quoted saying', citing this scene): Viola has left the text she was preaching on. Current 'You are now off your text' is not idiomatic; 'strayed from your text' keeps the image.
Archaic word order fixed: 'Is't not well done?' -> 'Isn't it well done?' (current 'Is it not'). 'well done' is kept because Viola's reply picks it up.

Kept from current: the first sentence ('commission' = warrant, authority: Onions 1911, commission 2) and 'draw the curtain and show you the picture'. The stage direction stays exactly as the current modern text has it.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. Excellently done — if God did all the painting.

units.o: Excellently done, if God did all.
units.m: Excellently done — if God did all the painting.

reasons: Joke made audible: 'if God did all' = if it is all natural, with no cosmetic paint. Viola stays inside Olivia's portrait conceit and hints that the 'picture' may be painted, which is why Olivia answers that the colour is 'in grain'. Current 'if God did all of it' leaves the cosmetics jab implicit; 'all the painting' carries both senses (painting a portrait, painting a face) without adding an explanation.

paragraphs.speaker: OLIVIA.
paragraphs.proposed: OLIVIA. It's dyed in the grain, sir, and won't wash off; it will endure wind and weather.

units.o: ’Tis in grain, sir;
units.m: It's dyed in the grain, sir, and won't wash off;

units.o: ’twill endure wind and weather.
units.m: it will endure wind and weather.

reasons: Technical gloss made clear: 'in grain' = dyed fast with grain (kermes), hence indelible and natural, not cosmetic (Onions 1911, grain 1, citing ''Tis in g., sir; 'twill endure wind and weather'; Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, grain: 'in g. == innate, natural, not factitious (used of colours)', Tw. I,5,255). Current 'fast-dyed' is a textile term many listeners will not decode, so the point (her colour is her own, not makeup) is lost. 'dyed in the grain ... won't wash off' keeps the dye image and states the point.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. It's beauty truly blended; its red and white were laid on by Nature's own sweet and skilful hand. Lady, you are the cruellest woman alive if you choose to lead these graces to the grave and leave the world no copy, no child to carry them on.

units.o: ’Tis beauty truly blent, whose red and white / Nature’s own sweet and cunning hand laid on.
units.m: It's beauty truly blended; its red and white were laid on by Nature's own sweet and skilful hand.

units.o: Lady, you are the cruel’st she alive / If you will lead these graces to the grave,
units.m: Lady, you are the cruellest woman alive if you choose to lead these graces to the grave

units.o: And leave the world no copy.
units.m: and leave the world no copy, no child to carry them on.

reasons: False friend fixed: 'cunning' = skilful, knowing (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, cunning adj. 1, citing 'whose red and white nature's own sweet and c. hand laid on', Tw. I,5,258; Onions 1911, cunning adj. 1 'skilful, clever'). Current keeps 'cunning', which a listener hears as 'sly', turning Viola's praise of natural beauty into a hint of trickery.

Pun set-up made audible: 'copy' = a reproduction, 'properly and tropically' (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, copy subst. 3, citing 'and leave the world no c.', Tw. I,5,261). Viola means a child who would reproduce these graces; Olivia's reply deliberately takes 'copy' and 'leave' as paperwork and a will. Current leaves 'no copy' unexplained; a short gloss states Viola's sense while the word stays for Olivia to twist.

'blent' = blended (Onions 1911, blent; Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, blend 1, Tw. I,5,257); current 'mixed' is acceptable, 'blended' keeps the painter's palette. 'If you will lead' -> 'if you lead': current 'if you would lead' turns Viola's warning into a remote hypothesis.

reviewer_fixes.find: if you lead these graces to the grave
reviewer_fixes.replace: if you choose to lead these graces to the grave
reviewer_fixes.reason: 'will' is volitional; Viola's charge of cruelty rests on the choice.

paragraphs.speaker: OLIVIA.
paragraphs.proposed: OLIVIA. Oh, sir, I won't be so hard-hearted. I'll issue several inventories of my beauty. It will be itemized, and every particle and utensil labelled and attached to my will, like this: item, two lips, fairly red; item, two grey eyes, complete with lids; item, one neck, one chin, and so on. Were you sent here to praise me — or to appraise me?

units.o: O, sir, I will not be so hard-hearted;
units.m: Oh, sir, I won't be so hard-hearted.

units.o: I will give out divers schedules of my beauty.
units.m: I'll issue several inventories of my beauty.

units.o: It shall be inventoried and every particle and utensil labelled to my will:
units.m: It will be itemized, and every particle and utensil labelled and attached to my will,

units.o: as, item, two lips indifferent red; item, two grey eyes with lids to them; item, one neck, one chin, and so forth.
units.m: like this: item, two lips, fairly red; item, two grey eyes, complete with lids; item, one neck, one chin, and so on.

units.o: Were you sent hither to praise me?
units.m: Were you sent here to praise me — or to appraise me?

reasons: Mis-gloss fixed: 'labelled to my will' = added to my will as a label or codicil (Onions 1911, label vb. 'to add as a "label" or codicil', citing 'every particle and utensil labelled to my will'; Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, label: 'a seal appended to a deed'). Current 'labelled by my will' reads as 'by my choice' and loses the joke that she will bequeath her beauty item by item, answering Viola's 'leave the world no copy'.

Flattened joke restored: 'utensil' = a household implement (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, utensil, citing Tw. I,5,264). Olivia lists her face like pots and pans in a probate inventory, hence eyes 'with lids to them'. Current 'feature' removes the joke; 'utensil' and 'complete with lids' (inventory language) restore it.

Pun restored: 'praise' also = appraise, value (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, praise vb. 4 'to appraise, to estimate: were you sent hither to p. me?', Tw. I,5,268; Onions 1911, praise vb. 'to appraise, value', same line). Current keeps only 'praise'; the listener now hears the valuer's sense that caps the inventory joke.

Kept from current: 'several inventories' ('divers schedules'; Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, schedule '== inventory' at Tw. I,5,263) and 'fairly red' ('indifferent red'; Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, indifferent adv. 'pretty, rather, somewhat', citing 'two lips i. red').

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. I see what you are: you are too proud. But even if you were the devil, you are beautiful. My lord and master loves you. Oh, even if you were crowned the unrivalled queen of beauty, you could do no more than repay such love!

units.o: I see you what you are, you are too proud;
units.m: I see what you are: you are too proud.

units.o: But, if you were the devil, you are fair.
units.m: But even if you were the devil, you are beautiful.

units.o: My lord and master loves you.
units.m: My lord and master loves you.

units.o: O, such love / Could be but recompens’d though you were crown’d / The nonpareil of beauty!
units.m: Oh, even if you were crowned the unrivalled queen of beauty, you could do no more than repay such love!

reasons: Misreading-prone syntax fixed: 'such love / Could be but recompens'd though you were crown'd / The nonpareil of beauty' = even if you were the peerless beauty, returning such love would merely repay it (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, recompense vb. 2 'to requite, to reward', Tw. I,5,272; Onions 1911, nonpareil 'one that has no equal', citing 'The n. of beauty'). Current 'such love could only be repaid even if you were crowned...' is heard as 'could only be repaid by something', and Viola's plea (love him back) is lost.
False friend fixed by ear: predicative 'you are fair' = you are beautiful; a listener hears 'fair' as 'just' or 'pale'. (The formulaic address 'fair cruelty' in 5.129 is kept.)
Idiom: 'I see you what you are' -> 'I see you for what you are' (current drops 'you').

reviewer_fixes.find: I see you for what you are
reviewer_fixes.reason: The original's 'you' is proleptic (Abbott §414); 'see you for what you are' adds a sneer. The current wording was more exact.

paragraphs.speaker: OLIVIA.
paragraphs.proposed: OLIVIA. How does he love me?

units.o: How does he love me?
units.m: How does he love me?

reasons: keep: already plain modern English.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. With adoration, abundant tears, with groans that thunder love, with sighs of fire.

units.o: With adorations, fertile tears, / With groans that thunder love, with sighs of fire.
units.m: With adoration, abundant tears, with groans that thunder love, with sighs of fire.

reasons: keep: 'fertile' is correctly glossed 'abundant' (Onions 1911, fertile 'abundant', citing 'f. tears', Tw.N. I.v.276); the images are already clear.

paragraphs.speaker: OLIVIA.
paragraphs.proposed: OLIVIA. Your lord knows my mind: I cannot love him. Yet I believe he is virtuous, and I know he is noble, of high rank and fortune, of fresh and stainless youth; well spoken of, generous, learned and brave; and in build and natural shape a handsome figure of a man. But still I cannot love him. He could have taken no for an answer long ago.

units.o: Your lord does know my mind, I cannot love him:
units.m: Your lord knows my mind: I cannot love him.

units.o: Yet I suppose him virtuous, know him noble, / Of great estate, of fresh and stainless youth;
units.m: Yet I believe he is virtuous, and I know he is noble, of high rank and fortune, of fresh and stainless youth;

units.o: In voices well divulg’d, free, learn’d, and valiant,
units.m: well spoken of, generous, learned and brave;

units.o: And in dimension and the shape of nature, / A gracious person.
units.m: and in build and natural shape a handsome figure of a man.

units.o: But yet I cannot love him.
units.m: But still I cannot love him.

units.o: He might have took his answer long ago.
units.m: He could have taken no for an answer long ago.

reasons: Mis-gloss fixed: 'free' = noble-minded, generous (Onions 1911, free adj. 1 'of noble or honourable character, generous, magnanimous', citing Tw.N. I.v.281; Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, free 11 'of a pure and generous mind', citing 'in voices well divulged, f., learned and valiant'). Current 'free-spirited' means unconventional or uninhibited, which is not the praise Olivia gives.

Meaning shift fixed: 'He might have took his answer' = he could have accepted my answer as final. Current 'He might have had his answer' says only that he received it; 'taken no for an answer' is the exact modern idiom.

Archaic words made clear: 'Of great estate' = of high rank (Onions 1911, estate sb. 2 'status, rank, dignity'), left as 'estate' (heard as landed property) in current; 'In voices well divulg'd' = of good repute (Onions 1911, divulge, and voice sb. 3 'general talk, rumour, report', both citing this line); 'dimension' = bodily frame (Onions 1911); 'A gracious person' = an attractive figure (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, gracious 5 'lovely, attractive, beautiful', citing 'a g. person', Tw. I,5,281; Onions 1911, person 1 'bodily figure'). Current 'a graceful person' weakens beauty to deportment.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. If I loved you with my master's flame, with such suffering, such a living death, I would find no sense in your refusal; I would not understand it.

units.o: If I did love you in my master’s flame, / With such a suff’ring, such a deadly life,
units.m: If I loved you with my master's flame, with such suffering, such a living death,

units.o: In your denial I would find no sense, / I would not understand it.
units.m: I would find no sense in your refusal; I would not understand it.

reasons: Meaning restored: 'I would not understand it' (the refusal would be meaningless to me). Current 'I would not accept it' substitutes defiance for incomprehension. 'sense' = meaning (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, sense, listing Tw. I,5,285 with 'he in the worst s. construes their denial').

Unidiomatic phrase fixed: 'such a deadly life' = a death-like life (Onions 1911, deadly adj. 'death-like, deathly', citing 'such a d. life'); current 'a dying life' is not English idiom; 'a living death' keeps the paradox.
Image restored: 'in my master's flame'; current 'with my master's passion' drops the fire.

paragraphs.speaker: OLIVIA.
paragraphs.proposed: OLIVIA. Why, what would you do?

units.o: Why, what would you?
units.m: Why, what would you do?

reasons: keep: the elliptical 'what would you?' is correctly completed.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. I'd make myself a willow cabin at your gate, like a forsaken lover, and call out to you, my soul, inside the house. I'd write faithful songs of scorned love and sing them loud even in the dead of night. I'd shout your name to the echoing hills and make the babbling gossip of the air cry out “Olivia!” Oh, you would find no rest anywhere between the elements of air and earth until you pitied me.

units.o: Make me a willow cabin at your gate, / And call upon my soul within the house;
units.m: I'd make myself a willow cabin at your gate, like a forsaken lover, and call out to you, my soul, inside the house.

units.o: Write loyal cantons of contemned love, / And sing them loud even in the dead of night;
units.m: I'd write faithful songs of scorned love and sing them loud even in the dead of night.

units.o: Hallow your name to the reverberate hills, / And make the babbling gossip of the air / Cry out Olivia!
units.m: I'd shout your name to the echoing hills and make the babbling gossip of the air cry out “Olivia!”

units.o: O, you should not rest / Between the elements of air and earth, / But you should pity me.
units.m: Oh, you would find no rest anywhere between the elements of air and earth until you pitied me.

reasons: Misleading by ear, fixed: 'Make me a willow cabin' = make myself a hut, answering 'what would you do?' (Onions 1911, cabin sb. 1 'temporary shelter of slight materials', citing 'a willow cabin'). Current keeps 'Make me...', which a listener hears as an order to Olivia. 'I'd make myself a willow cabin at your gate' keeps the famous line recognizable.

Opaque allusion clarified: willow = emblem of disappointed love (Onions 1911, willow 'w. garland, emblem of disappointed love'); a few words added. 'call upon my soul within the house': the soul is Olivia, so 'call out to you, my soul' unpacks it.

'cantons' = songs (Onions 1911, canton, citing 'Write loyal cantons'); 'contemned' = scornfully refused (Onions 1911, contemn). Current 'loyal songs of rejected love' is acceptable; 'faithful songs of scorned love' is closer and more natural.

Archaic word fixed: 'Hallow' = shout (Onions 1911, hallow 'to shout ... once trans. Tw.N. I.v.293'; Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon lists this line under Holla vb. 2 'to cry loudly' and Hollo vb. 'to utter loudly' (O. Edd. hallow), not under Hallow 'to make holy', so no 'holy' pun is imported). Current 'Halloo' is a hunting cry most listeners will not parse. 'reverberate' = resounding (Onions 1911); 'babbling gossip' = tattler (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, gossip subst. 3, citing 'the babbling g. of the air'); after 'echoing hills' the echo is clear, so no gloss is added.

False friend fixed: 'you should not rest ... But you should pity me', where 'should' = would. Current 'you should find no rest' is heard as 'ought to'. 'the elements of air and earth' kept (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, element 2, citing this line).
Convention fixed: current quotes the cry in single curly quotes; Standard rule 8 requires curly double quotes.

reviewer_fixes.find: I'd make myself a willow cabin at your gate — willow, the tree of rejected lovers — and call out to you, my soul, inside the house.
reviewer_fixes.replace: I'd make myself a willow cabin at your gate, like a forsaken lover, and call out to you, my soul, inside the house.
reviewer_fixes.reason: The gloss (willow = emblem of forsaken love: Furness; Onions) was a footnote-style aside in Viola's most famous speech; folded into her own plea. The TN blind reader made the same point.

paragraphs.speaker: OLIVIA.
paragraphs.proposed: OLIVIA. You might do much. What is your parentage?

units.o: You might do much.
units.m: You might do much.

units.o: What is your parentage?
units.m: What is your parentage?

reasons: keep: plain modern English; 'You might do much' stays deliberately open (Standard rule 7), so no gloss.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. My birth is above my present fortunes, yet my standing is good: I am a gentleman.

units.o: Above my fortunes, yet my state is well: / I am a gentleman.
units.m: My birth is above my present fortunes, yet my standing is good: I am a gentleman.

reasons: Opaque answer made clear: to 'What is your parentage?', 'Above my fortunes' = my birth is higher than my present lot (a servant's), and 'state' = rank, standing. Current 'Above my fortunes, yet my situation is good' leaves the first phrase opaque and blurs rank into circumstances; 'present' and 'standing' make the class point audible.
Olivia repeats this line word for word at 5.131 (outside the passage); the echo there must use whatever wording 5.127 adopts (see structure_notes).

reviewer_fixes.replace: My birth is above my present fortunes
reviewer_fixes.reason: The fragment needed its subject; Olivia repeats the line at 5.131, so it must stand alone.

paragraphs.speaker: OLIVIA.
paragraphs.proposed: OLIVIA. Get yourself back to your lord. I cannot love him. Let him send no more — unless, perhaps, you come to me again to tell me how he takes it. Farewell. I thank you for your trouble. Take this, and spend it for my sake.

units.o: Get you to your lord; / I cannot love him:
units.m: Get yourself back to your lord. I cannot love him.

units.o: let him send no more, / Unless, perchance, you come to me again, / To tell me how he takes it.
units.m: Let him send no more — unless, perhaps, you come to me again to tell me how he takes it.

units.o: Fare you well:
units.m: Farewell.

units.o: I thank you for your pains: spend this for me.
units.m: I thank you for your trouble. Take this, and spend it for my sake.

reasons: Ambiguity fixed: 'spend this for me': she offers money (Viola answers 'keep your purse'); 'spend' = lay out, expend (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, spend 5, citing Tw. I,5,302). Current 'Spend this for me' sounds like an errand on her behalf; 'spend it for my sake' makes it a tip. The rest of the current paragraph is kept word for word.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. I am no paid messenger, lady; keep your purse. It is my master, not I, who goes unrepaid. May Love give the man you come to love a heart of flint, and may your passion, like my master's, be met with contempt. Farewell, fair cruelty.

units.o: I am no fee’d post, lady; keep your purse;
units.m: I am no paid messenger, lady; keep your purse.

units.o: My master, not myself, lacks recompense.
units.m: It is my master, not I, who goes unrepaid.

units.o: Love make his heart of flint that you shall love,
units.m: May Love give the man you come to love a heart of flint,

units.o: And let your fervour like my master’s be / Plac’d in contempt.
units.m: and may your passion, like my master's, be met with contempt.

units.o: Farewell, fair cruelty.
units.m: Farewell, fair cruelty.

reasons: Unnatural syntax fixed: 'Love make his heart of flint that you shall love' = may Love harden to flint the heart of the man you will love. Current 'May Love make hard as flint the heart of whomever you fall in love with' inverts the clause, is hard to follow by ear, and drops the original's 'his' (a man).

Stiff phrase fixed: 'lacks recompense' = goes without requital or reward (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, recompense subst. 2 'requital, reward', citing Tw. I,5,304). 'fee'd post' = paid messenger (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, post subst. 2 'a messenger', citing Tw. I,5,303), kept from current.
'Farewell, fair cruelty' kept: famous, and 'fair' in a formulaic address is heard as 'beautiful'.

structure_notes: o_lines use the packet's '|' lines: Gutenberg verse lines, with each prose run counted as one line. Prose paragraphs (5.114, 5.118) therefore map every unit to [1, 1]. Where a sentence ends mid-line (5.119, 5.122, 5.125, 5.128, 5.129), adjacent units share that line number. Each unit carries an extra field 'o' quoting the exact original words it renders.
5.114: the stage direction [_Unveiling._] sits inside Olivia's prose paragraph. It is kept in place exactly as the current modern text has it ('[Unveiling.]').
5.126 holds two half-lines of verse ('You might do much. / What is your parentage?'); mapped as two units.

5.127 is quoted word for word by Olivia at 5.131 (outside this passage). Current 5.131 quotes the untranslated original ('Above my fortunes, yet my state is well: I am a gentleman.') in single curly quotes, while current 5.127 modernizes it, so the echo is already broken. Whatever wording 5.127 adopts must be reused verbatim, in curly double quotes, at 5.131.
Convention: the live modern text uses curly apostrophes (U+2019) throughout. All proposed text, including 'keep' paragraphs, uses straight apostrophes (Standard rule 8); 'keep' means no word changes.
current_defects: 5.114: unnatural syntax, joke lost: 'Look, sir, just like this I was at this present time' keeps the inverted order of 'such a one I was this present' (= how I looked at this very moment, like a dated portrait label; Schmidt present subst. 2, Onions present sb. 2).
5.114: unidiomatic: 'You are now off your text' for the sermon image 'out of your text'.
5.115: joke flattened: 'if God did all of it' leaves the cosmetics jab (face paint as against portrait paint) implicit.
5.116: technical gloss too opaque: 'fast-dyed' for 'in grain' (natural, indelible colour); the point that her colour is not makeup is lost.
5.117: false friend left: 'cunning' (= skilful; Schmidt cunning adj. 1, Onions cunning adj. 1) is heard as 'sly'.

5.117: pun set-up not audible: 'leave the world no copy' (a child; Schmidt copy subst. 3) is unexplained, so Olivia's inventory twist in 5.118 has nothing to push against. Also 'if you would lead' weakens 'If you will lead'.
5.118: mis-gloss: 'labelled by my will' for 'labelled to my will' (appended to my will as a codicil; Onions label vb.).
5.118: joke flattened: 'utensil' (household implement; Schmidt utensil) rendered 'feature'.
5.118: pun dropped: 'praise' = praise and appraise (Schmidt praise vb. 4; Onions praise vb., both citing this line).
5.119: misreading-prone syntax: 'such love could only be repaid even if you were crowned...' hides 'even the peerless beauty could do no more than repay such love'.
5.119: false friend by ear: predicative 'you are fair' (beautiful) is heard as 'just' or 'pale'.
5.122: mis-gloss: 'free-spirited' for 'free' (= noble-minded, generous; Onions free adj. 1, Schmidt free 11, both citing this line).
5.122: meaning shift: 'He might have had his answer' for 'might have took his answer' (accepted it as final).
5.122: archaic words left or weakened: 'of great estate' (= high rank); 'a graceful person' for 'a gracious person' (an attractive figure; Schmidt gracious 5).
5.123: meaning changed: 'I would not accept it' for 'I would not understand it'; unidiomatic 'a dying life' for 'deadly life' (death-like; Onions); the fire of 'flame' dropped.
5.125: misleading by ear: 'Make me a willow cabin' is heard as an order to Olivia; willow symbolism (disappointed love) left unexplained.
5.125: archaic word left: 'Halloo' for 'Hallow' (= shout; Onions hallow, Schmidt holla/hollo).
5.125: false friend: 'you should find no rest' ('should' = would) is heard as 'ought to'.
5.125: convention: the cry is quoted in single curly quotes; the Standard requires curly double quotes.
5.127: opaque: 'Above my fortunes, yet my situation is good' leaves the class point unclear; the line is echoed at 5.131, where current quotes the untranslated original instead.
5.128: ambiguous: 'Spend this for me' sounds like an errand; it is a tip.
5.129: unnatural syntax: 'May Love make hard as flint the heart of whomever you fall in love with' (inverted; drops 'his').
All TN-A paragraphs: convention: curly apostrophes (U+2019) throughout; Standard rule 8 requires straight apostrophes.

paragraphs.proposed: [Enter Viola and Clown with a tabor.]

units.o: Enter Viola and Clown with a tabor.
units.m: [Enter Viola and Clown with a tabor.]

reasons: Stage direction kept exactly as the current modern text has it.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. God save you, friend, and your music. Do you live by your tabor?

units.o: Save thee, friend, and thy music.
units.m: God save you, friend, and your music.

units.o: Dost thou live by thy tabor?
units.m: Do you live by your tabor?

reasons: keep: 'live by' still carries both senses Feste needs (earn a living by / live next to; Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, live vb., citing 'dost thou l. by thy tabor?' for the first and 'I l. by the church' for 'to abide, to dwell'); 'tabor' is identified as an instrument by 'music' and the stage direction.

paragraphs.speaker: CLOWN.
paragraphs.proposed: CLOWN. No, sir, I live by the church.

units.o: No, sir, I live by the church.
units.m: No, sir, I live by the church.

reasons: keep: the pun works unchanged.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. Are you a churchman?

units.o: Art thou a churchman?
units.m: Are you a churchman?

reasons: keep: 'churchman' (clergyman) is current English.

paragraphs.speaker: CLOWN.
paragraphs.proposed: CLOWN. No such thing, sir. I live by the church, because I live at my house, and my house stands by the church.

units.o: No such matter, sir.
units.m: No such thing, sir.

units.o: I do live by the church, for I do live at my house, and my house doth stand by the church.
units.m: I live by the church, because I live at my house, and my house stands by the church.

reasons: keep: clear, and the 'by' joke is intact.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. So you might as well say the king lies by a beggar, if a beggar lives near him; or that the church stands by your tabor, if your tabor stands by the church.

units.o: So thou mayst say the king lies by a beggar, if a beggar dwell near him;
units.m: So you might as well say the king lies by a beggar, if a beggar lives near him;

units.o: or the church stands by thy tabor, if thy tabor stand by the church.
units.m: or that the church stands by your tabor, if your tabor stands by the church.

reasons: Wordplay made audible: 'lies by' = lodges, sleeps beside (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, lie vb., the lodging sense, citing 'the king --s by a beggar', Tw. III,1,8; Onions 1911, lie 4 'to dwell, sojourn, lodge, esp. to sleep or pass the night somewhere'). Current keeps 'lies by', which a listener now hears as 'tells lies', so Viola's absurd picture (the king in bed beside a beggar) is lost. 'stands by' keeps both senses in modern English (is next to / supports) and is unchanged.
Register: 'So thou mayst say' -> 'So you might as well say', so the listener hears Viola mocking Feste's logic with his own trick.

reviewer_fixes.find: the king sleeps beside a beggar
reviewer_fixes.replace: the king lies by a beggar
reviewer_fixes.reason: 'lies' = lodges, dwells (Schmidt lie vb. 7, citing this line; Malone in Furness), with the lie/lie quibble; 'sleeps beside' narrowed it to a bed image.

paragraphs.speaker: CLOWN.
paragraphs.proposed: CLOWN. You have said it, sir. What an age this is! A sentence is just a kidskin glove to a sharp wit — how quickly the wrong side can be turned outward!

units.o: You have said, sir.
units.m: You have said it, sir.

units.o: To see this age!
units.m: What an age this is!

units.o: A sentence is but a chev’ril glove to a good wit.
units.m: A sentence is just a kidskin glove to a sharp wit —

units.o: How quickly the wrong side may be turned outward!
units.m: how quickly the wrong side can be turned outward!

reasons: keep: 'chev'ril' is correctly glossed as kidskin (Onions 1911, cheveril 'kid-leather; always used allusively as a type of flexibility', citing Tw.N. III.i.13); the glove image and its point (a sentence turned inside out; Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, side: 'to turn the wrong s. out == to pervert, to distort', citing this line) are clear.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. No doubt — those who toy cleverly with words can quickly make them loose.

units.o: Nay, that’s certain;
units.m: No doubt —

units.o: they that dally nicely with words may quickly make them wanton.
units.m: those who toy cleverly with words can quickly make them loose.

reasons: Pun made audible: 'wanton' = 'loose, light, trifling' and 'lustful, lascivious' (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, wanton adj. 2 and 4, listing Tw. III,1,18 under 4; Onions 1911, wanton adj., ''lascivious' the most freq. sense'). Viola means words become slippery in meaning; Feste (11.10) takes it as 'unchaste'. Current keeps 'wanton', whose double sense a listener does not hear; 'loose' carries both (loose meaning, loose morals) and feeds 11.10.

Archaic verb replaced: 'dally' = trifle, toy (Onions 1911, dally, citing III.i.16), left as 'dally' in current. 'nicely' = subtly (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, nicely 3 'sophistically, subtilely', citing this line; Onions 1911 gives 'elegantly, daintily'): current 'cleverly' is kept.

paragraphs.speaker: CLOWN.
paragraphs.proposed: CLOWN. So I wish, sir, my sister had had no name.

units.o: I would, therefore, my sister had had no name, sir.
units.m: So I wish, sir, my sister had had no name.

reasons: keep: plain; sets up the joke.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. Why, man?

units.o: Why, man?
units.m: Why, man?

reasons: keep.

paragraphs.speaker: CLOWN.
paragraphs.proposed: CLOWN. Why, sir, her name is a word, and toying with that word might make my sister loose. But truly, words have been downright rascals since bonds disgraced them.

units.o: Why, sir, her name’s a word; and to dally with that word might make my sister wanton.
units.m: Why, sir, her name is a word, and toying with that word might make my sister loose.

units.o: But indeed, words are very rascals, since bonds disgraced them.
units.m: But truly, words have been downright rascals since bonds disgraced them.

reasons: Pun carried through from 11.7: 'dally ... wanton' -> 'toying ... loose', so the listener hears Feste turn Viola's remark into a joke about his sister's chastity. Current 'dallying ... wanton' leaves both words archaic.

Jargon replaced: 'since bonds disgraced them' = since a man's word needs a signed bond before anyone trusts it (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, bond, listing Tw. III,1,25 with the deed sense; Onions 1911, bond 4 'deed by which one binds oneself to another to make a payment or fulfil a contract'). Current 'promissory bonds' is legal jargon a listener will not parse; 'written bonds' makes the point and keeps the word, whose other sense (fetters, fit for rascals; Onions 1911, bond 1) still sounds.

reviewer_fixes.find: ever since written bonds disgraced them
reviewer_fixes.reason: A recorded crux: bonds = confinement and money bonds (Deighton), limits and contracts (Chambers) (Furness: 'dark passage'). Plain 'bonds' keeps both senses; 'since' may be temporal or causal.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. Your reasoning, man?

units.o: Thy reason, man?
units.m: Your reasoning, man?

reasons: keep: clear, and Feste's 'reason' echo still works.

paragraphs.speaker: CLOWN.
paragraphs.proposed: CLOWN. Truly, sir, I can give you none without words, and words have become so false that I am loath to use them to prove a reason.

units.o: Troth, sir, I can yield you none without words,
units.m: Truly, sir, I can give you none without words,

units.o: and words are grown so false, I am loath to prove reason with them.
units.m: and words have become so false that I am loath to use them to prove a reason.

reasons: Unidiomatic phrase fixed: 'prove reason with them' = make a reasoned demonstration with them (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, prove f 'to evince or establish as a truth, to demonstrate', citing Tw. III,1,29). Current 'argue reason with them' is not English idiom; 'reason with them' is natural and keeps the echo of Viola's 'reason'. The rest of current is kept.

reviewer_fixes.find: that I am loath to reason with them.
reviewer_fixes.replace: that I am loath to use them to prove a reason.
reviewer_fixes.reason: 'prove reason with them' = demonstrate a reason by words (Schmidt prove f); 'reason with them' is heard as persuading someone.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. I'll wager you are a merry fellow, and care for nothing.

units.o: I warrant thou art a merry fellow, and car’st for nothing.
units.m: I'll wager you are a merry fellow, and care for nothing.

reasons: keep: 'care for' still carries both senses Feste plays on (worry about / be fond of).

paragraphs.speaker: CLOWN.
paragraphs.proposed: CLOWN. Not so, sir — I do care for something. But in my conscience, sir, I don't care for you. If that means caring for nothing, sir, I wish it would make you invisible.

units.o: Not so, sir, I do care for something.
units.m: Not so, sir — I do care for something.

units.o: But in my conscience, sir, I do not care for you.
units.m: But in my conscience, sir, I don't care for you.

units.o: If that be to care for nothing, sir, I would it would make you invisible.
units.m: If that means caring for nothing, sir, I wish it would make you invisible.

reasons: keep: the insult (you are nothing, so be invisible) is clear.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. Aren't you Lady Olivia's fool?

units.o: Art not thou the Lady Olivia’s fool?
units.m: Aren't you Lady Olivia's fool?

reasons: keep: 'fool' (jester) must stay for Feste's fool/folly/husband joke.

paragraphs.speaker: CLOWN.
paragraphs.proposed: CLOWN. No, indeed, sir. Lady Olivia has no folly. She'll keep no fool, sir, until she's married — and fools are as like husbands as pilchards are to herrings: the husband is the bigger one. I am indeed not her fool, but her corrupter of words.

units.o: No, indeed, sir; the Lady Olivia has no folly.
units.m: No, indeed, sir. Lady Olivia has no folly.

units.o: She will keep no fool, sir, till she be married,
units.m: She'll keep no fool, sir, until she's married —

units.o: and fools are as like husbands as pilchards are to herrings, the husband’s the bigger.
units.m: and fools are as like husbands as pilchards are to herrings: the husband is the bigger one.

units.o: I am indeed not her fool, but her corrupter of words.
units.m: I am indeed not her fool, but her corrupter of words.

reasons: Archaic syntax fixed: current keeps the subjunctive 'till she be married'. Everything else is kept word for word; the folly/fool play and the pilchard-herring comparison (a husband is just a bigger fool) are already clear.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. I saw you recently at Count Orsino's.

units.o: I saw thee late at the Count Orsino’s.
units.m: I saw you recently at Count Orsino's.

reasons: keep: 'late' correctly rendered 'recently'.

paragraphs.speaker: CLOWN.
paragraphs.proposed: CLOWN. Foolery, sir, walks around the world like the sun — it shines everywhere. I would be sorry, sir, if the fool weren't as often with your master as with my mistress. I think I saw your wise self there.

units.o: Foolery, sir, does walk about the orb like the sun; it shines everywhere.
units.m: Foolery, sir, walks around the world like the sun — it shines everywhere.

units.o: I would be sorry, sir, but the fool should be as oft with your master as with my mistress.
units.m: I would be sorry, sir, if the fool weren't as often with your master as with my mistress.

units.o: I think I saw your wisdom there.
units.m: I think I saw your wise self there.

reasons: Joke made audible: 'your wisdom' is an ironic way of saying 'you' (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, wisdom 2, citing Tw. III,1,47), implying that the fool Feste saw at Orsino's was Viola. Current 'I saw your wisdom there' sounds by ear like an abstract quality; 'your wise self' keeps the irony and points at Viola, which prompts her retort in 11.19.

Substitution fixed: 'Foolery' (the fool's trade, jesting) restored; current 'Folly' shifts it to foolishness. The rest of current is kept, including the double sense of 'the fool' (Feste himself / folly in Orsino).

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. No — if you're going to take jabs at me, I'm done with you. Here, take this for your expenses.

units.o: Nay, and thou pass upon me, I’ll no more with thee.
units.m: No — if you're going to take jabs at me, I'm done with you.

units.o: Hold, there’s expenses for thee.
units.m: Here, take this for your expenses.

reasons: Image restored: 'pass upon me' is a fencing thrust used figuratively (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, pass vb. 9 'to thrust, to make a push in fencing ... Figuratively: an thou p. upon me, I'll no more with thee, Tw. III,1,48 (if thou makest sallies of wit on my score)'). Current 'if you start mocking me' is right in sense but drops the thrust; 'take jabs at me' is the modern idiom with the same image. Minor. The second sentence is kept from current.

paragraphs.speaker: CLOWN.
paragraphs.proposed: CLOWN. Now may Jove, in his next shipment of hair, send you a beard!

units.o: Now Jove, in his next commodity of hair, send thee a beard!
units.m: Now may Jove, in his next shipment of hair, send you a beard!

reasons: keep: 'commodity' is correctly glossed as a consignment of goods (Onions 1911, commodity 4 'quantity of wares, parcel, consignment, lot', citing 'his next c. of hair'); Jove kept as named.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. Upon my word, I'll tell you — I'm almost sick with longing for one, though I wouldn't want it to grow on my chin. Is your lady within?

units.o: By my troth, I’ll tell thee, I am almost sick for one,
units.m: Upon my word, I'll tell you — I'm almost sick with longing for one,

units.o: though I would not have it grow on my chin.
units.m: though I wouldn't want it to grow on my chin.

units.o: Is thy lady within?
units.m: Is your lady within?

reasons: Archaic oath rendered as an oath: 'By my troth' (troth = truth, faith: Onions 1911, troth 1-2) is left untranslated in current; 'Upon my word' keeps it an oath (Standard rule 8).

Double meaning made audible: 'sick for one' = pining for one (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, sick, 'with for, == pining for ... s. for one (beard) Tw. III,1,53'), a beard, and secretly the bearded Orsino, which is why she would not have it grow on her own chin. Current 'sick for one' is not modern idiom and the lovesick sense is faint; 'sick with longing' carries it.
'within' -> 'in' (at home).

reviewer_fixes.reason: Feste's delayed answer 'My lady is within, sir' (11.26) depends on the word; 'within' is still plain English.

paragraphs.speaker: CLOWN.
paragraphs.proposed: CLOWN. Wouldn't a pair of these coins have bred, sir?

units.o: Would not a pair of these have bred, sir?
units.m: Wouldn't a pair of these coins have bred, sir?

reasons: Unclear without the stage picture, fixed: 'these' = the coin Viola has just given him, which a listener cannot see. Feste begs a second coin by joking that a pair would breed; 'coins' is added so the money joke is heard.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. Yes, if they were kept together and put to use — lent out at interest.

units.o: Yes, being kept together, and put to use.
units.m: Yes, if they were kept together and put to use — lent out at interest.

reasons: Pun restored: 'put to use' = lent at interest (Onions 1911, use sb. 4 'interest on something lent ... phr. put to use Tw.N. III.i.58'). Current 'put to use' is heard only as 'used', so the usury joke (money breeding money) disappears; a short appositive restores it, while 'kept together ... put to use' keeps the breeding-pair sense.

structure_notes: 11.0: the original-en edition carries this stage direction unbracketed and without italic markers ('Enter Viola and Clown with a tabor.'), unlike later directions ('[_Exit._]'); current modern-en bracketed it. Kept exactly as the current modern text has it.
All TN-B paragraphs are prose (one packet line each), so every unit is [1, 1] and is identified by its 'o' field.

Chained wordplay: 11.7 ('loose') feeds 11.10 ('loose'), and 11.22 ('coins ... bred') feeds 11.23 ('put to use ... interest'). Review these pairs together; changing one without the other breaks the joke.
Convention: curly apostrophes normalized to straight in all proposed text, including 'keep' paragraphs (11.13, 11.14, 11.15, 11.17); no word changes in those.
current_defects: 11.5: pun lost by ear: 'the king lies by a beggar' keeps 'lies by' (= lodges, sleeps beside; Schmidt lie vb., Onions lie 4), which a listener now hears as 'tells lies'.

11.7: archaic words left, pun not audible: 'dally' and 'wanton' (Schmidt wanton adj. 2 'loose, light, trifling' and 4 'lustful, lascivious', citing this line); the slippery/unchaste double sense that 11.10 exploits is not heard.
11.10: same pun left archaic ('dallying ... wanton'); legal jargon 'promissory bonds' for 'bonds' (the written bonds that replaced trust in a man's word).
11.12: unidiomatic: 'argue reason with them' for 'prove reason with them'.
11.16: archaic subjunctive left: 'till she be married'.
11.18: joke unclear by ear: 'I think I saw your wisdom there' (ironic for Viola herself) is heard as an abstract quality; 'Foolery' shifted to 'Folly'.
11.19: image dropped (minor): 'pass upon me' (a fencing thrust, figuratively sallies of wit at my expense; Schmidt pass vb. 9) flattened to 'mocking me'.
11.21: archaic oath left untranslated: 'By my troth'; 'sick for one' is not modern idiom and the lovesick double meaning is faint.
11.22: unclear without the stage picture: 'a pair of these' (coins).
11.23: pun lost: 'put to use' (lent at interest; Onions use sb. 4, citing this line) is heard only as 'used', so the money-breeding joke disappears.
All TN-B paragraphs: convention: curly apostrophes throughout.

paragraphs.speaker: DUKE.
paragraphs.proposed: DUKE. Let all the rest withdraw.

units.o: Let all the rest give place.
units.m: Let all the rest withdraw.

reasons: keep: 'give place' is correctly rendered 'withdraw'.

paragraphs.proposed: [Exeunt Curio and Attendants.]

units.o: [_Exeunt Curio and Attendants._]
units.m: [Exeunt Curio and Attendants.]

reasons: Stage direction kept exactly as the current modern text has it.

paragraphs.proposed: Once more, Cesario, go to that same queen of cruelty. Tell her my love, nobler than the world, sets no value on any quantity of dirty land. The gifts that Fortune has bestowed on her, tell her I hold as carelessly as Fortune does. But what draws my soul is that miracle, that queen of jewels Nature has decked her out in: her beauty.

units.o: Once more, Cesario, / Get thee to yond same sovereign cruelty.
units.m: Once more, Cesario, go to that same queen of cruelty.

units.o: Tell her my love, more noble than the world, / Prizes not quantity of dirty lands;
units.m: Tell her my love, nobler than the world, sets no value on any quantity of dirty land.

units.o: The parts that fortune hath bestow’d upon her, / Tell her I hold as giddily as fortune;
units.m: The gifts that Fortune has bestowed on her, tell her I hold as carelessly as Fortune does.

units.o: But ’tis that miracle and queen of gems / That nature pranks her in attracts my soul.
units.m: But what draws my soul is that miracle, that queen of jewels Nature has decked her out in: her beauty.

reasons: Mis-gloss fixed: 'dirty lands' = filthy land, said in contempt (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, dirty 'nasty, filthy', citing Tw. II,4,85; Onions 1911, dirty 'as an epithet of disgust or aversion'). Current 'common land' names a legal category (land held in common) and drops the contempt for her estates.

Non-word and false friend fixed: 'giddily' = carelessly, heedlessly (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, giddily 2, citing 'the parts that fortune hath bestowed upon her, I hold as g. as fortune'); current coins 'fickly', which is not English. 'parts' = endowments, gifts (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, part 4 'that which is bestowed upon one, gift, endowment', citing Tw. II,4,86; Onions 1911, part sb. 3), here Fortune's gifts as against Nature's gift in the next sentence; current keeps 'parts', which a listener hears as body parts.

Hard metaphor made clear in the same sentence: 'that miracle and queen of gems / That nature pranks her in' = the jewel Nature has decked her out in, her beauty (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, prank vb. 'to deck, to dress up, to adorn', citing this line). Current leaves the metaphor unexplained.

Personification made audible: 'sovereign cruelty' = supreme Cruelty, i.e. Olivia (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, sovereign 2 'supreme, paramount, excellent', citing 'yond same s. cruelty'). Current keeps the abstraction, which by ear does not sound like a person; 'queen of cruelty' names her as the supreme example, matching Orsino's own royal imagery ('queen of gems'). 'Get thee' -> 'go'.
Parser fragment: no speaker prefix, kept as in the current text (see structure_notes).

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. But what if she cannot love you, sir?

units.o: But if she cannot love you, sir?
units.m: But what if she cannot love you, sir?

reasons: keep.

paragraphs.speaker: DUKE.
paragraphs.proposed: DUKE. I cannot accept such an answer.

units.o: I cannot be so answer’d.
units.m: I cannot accept such an answer.

reasons: keep: 'be so answer'd' = accept that answer; correctly rendered, and now echoed in 9.39.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. But truly, you must. Say that some lady — as perhaps there is — feels as great a heartache for love of you as you feel for Olivia. You cannot love her; you tell her so. Then mustn't she accept that answer?

units.o: Sooth, but you must.
units.m: But truly, you must.

units.o: Say that some lady, as perhaps there is, / Hath for your love as great a pang of heart / As you have for Olivia:
units.m: Say that some lady — as perhaps there is — feels as great a heartache for love of you as you feel for Olivia.

units.o: you cannot love her; / You tell her so.
units.m: You cannot love her; you tell her so.

units.o: Must she not then be answer’d?
units.m: Then mustn't she accept that answer?

reasons: Persuasion restored: 'Must she not then be answer'd?' turns Orsino's own words ('I cannot be so answer'd', 9.38) back on him; 'be answered' = accept the answer. Current 'Must she not then be given her answer?' changes the sense (receive, not accept) and breaks the echo with 9.38 'I cannot accept such an answer'.
'Sooth' = truly, an asseveration (Onions 1911, sooth 1); current 'Truly, but you must' can be heard as a concession ('True, but'). 'pang of heart' -> 'heartache'; archaic 'Must she not' reordered.

paragraphs.speaker: DUKE.
paragraphs.proposed: DUKE. No woman's ribs can bear the pounding of so strong a passion as love gives my heart; no woman's heart is big enough to hold so much; they cannot retain it. Alas, their love may be called appetite — not a stirring of the liver, the seat of passion, but of the palate — an appetite that is glutted, grows sick of the taste, and revolts in disgust. But mine is every bit as hungry as the sea, and can digest as much. Make no comparison between the love a woman can bear me and the love I bear Olivia.

units.o: There is no woman’s sides / Can bide the beating of so strong a passion / As love doth give my heart:
units.m: No woman's ribs can bear the pounding of so strong a passion as love gives my heart;

units.o: no woman’s heart / So big, to hold so much; they lack retention.
units.m: no woman's heart is big enough to hold so much; they cannot retain it.

units.o: Alas, their love may be called appetite, / No motion of the liver, but the palate, / That suffer surfeit, cloyment, and revolt;
units.m: Alas, their love may be called appetite — not a stirring of the liver, the seat of passion, but of the palate — an appetite that is glutted, grows sick of the taste, and revolts in disgust.

units.o: But mine is all as hungry as the sea, / And can digest as much.
units.m: But mine is every bit as hungry as the sea, and can digest as much.

units.o: Make no compare / Between that love a woman can bear me / And that I owe Olivia.
units.m: Make no comparison between the love a woman can bear me and the love I bear Olivia.

reasons: False friend fixed: 'revolt' = revulsion of appetite (Onions 1911, revolt sb. 3, citing Tw.N. II.iv.101). Current keeps the noun 'revolt', heard as rebellion; 'revolts in disgust' uses the modern stomach sense.

Hard list made followable: 'surfeit' = excess in eating and the sickness and satiety it causes (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, surfeit subst., citing 'suffer s., cloyment and revolt'); 'cloyment' = satiety (Onions 1911, cloyment, same line). Current 'which suffers gluttony, satiation, and revolt' is a word list that is hard to follow by ear ('suffers gluttony' is not idiomatic); rendered as a sequence of eating verbs.

Opaque allusion clarified: 'liver' = the supposed seat of love and violent passion (Onions 1911, liver, citing Orsino's own 'liver, brain, and heart' in 1.1); current 'no movement of the liver' leaves it opaque. 'motion' = inward stirring (Onions 1911, motion sb. 5).

Parallel restored: 'that I owe Olivia': to owe a person love = to bear love (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, owe, 'with a dative and accusative ... == to bear love or hate', citing this line and Viola's reply). Current 'what I feel for Olivia' breaks Orsino's parallel (love a woman can bear me / love I bear Olivia), which Viola answers in 9.43. Modern 'owe' would add a sense of debt, so 'bear' is used.

'they lack retention' = they cannot hold on to it (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, retention 1 'the power ... of preserving', Onions 1911 'capacity for holding', both citing this line). Current 'They lack capacity' is defensible but repeats the size point just made; 'cannot retain it' adds the keeping that Orsino's claim needs. 'sides' = the body's sides that hold the heart (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, side 1); 'bide' = endure (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, bide 2a, citing Tw. II,4,97). Current 'body' is acceptable; 'ribs' keeps the pounding image. Minor.
Small omission fixed: 'mine is all as hungry as the sea' — current drops the intensifier 'all'; 'every bit as hungry' restores it.

reviewer_fixes.find: but of the palate, which overeats, grows sick of the taste, and revolts in disgust.
reviewer_fixes.replace: but of the palate — an appetite that is glutted, grows sick of the taste, and revolts in disgust.
reviewer_fixes.reason: Crux 'That suffer surfeit': taken as appetite, after Deighton and Furness (Malone and Innes refer the plural 'suffer' to women). The draft made 'palate' the subject, a reading no Variorum commentator gives; 'overeats' also made 'suffer surfeit' active.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. Yes, but I know —

units.o: Ay, but I know—
units.m: Yes, but I know —

reasons: keep: interruption kept as a spaced em dash.

paragraphs.speaker: DUKE.
paragraphs.proposed: DUKE. What do you know?

units.o: What dost thou know?
units.m: What do you know?

reasons: keep.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. Only too well what love women may bear to men. In truth, they are as true of heart as we are. My father had a daughter who loved a man, as I might perhaps love your lordship, if I were a woman.

units.o: Too well what love women to men may owe.
units.m: Only too well what love women may bear to men.

units.o: In faith, they are as true of heart as we.
units.m: In truth, they are as true of heart as we are.

units.o: My father had a daughter loved a man, / As it might be perhaps, were I a woman, / I should your lordship.
units.m: My father had a daughter who loved a man, as I might perhaps love your lordship, if I were a woman.

reasons: Archaic syntax fixed: 'As it might be perhaps, were I a woman, / I should your lordship' = as I, perhaps, might love your lordship if I were a woman ('should' = would). Current keeps the inverted order ('as it might be perhaps, were I a woman, I should love your lordship'), which is hard to follow by ear and makes 'should' sound like obligation. The dramatic irony stays.

'owe' = bear (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, owe, citing 'what love women to men may o.'). Current 'Too well, what love women may bear men' is right in sense, but the stray comma breaks the answer and 'bear men' can be misheard (give birth to men); 'bear to men' fixes both and keeps the echo of Orsino's 'bear' in 9.40. 'Only too well' is the natural intensifier.

paragraphs.speaker: DUKE.
paragraphs.proposed: DUKE. And what is her history?

units.o: And what’s her history?
units.m: And what is her history?

reasons: keep.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. A blank, my lord. She never told her love, but let concealment, like a worm in the bud, feed on her rosy cheek. She pined away in silent longing, and with a green and yellow melancholy she sat like Patience carved on a monument, smiling at grief. Wasn't this love indeed? We men may say more, swear more, but in fact our show is greater than what we really feel; for we always prove much in our vows, but little in our love.

units.o: A blank, my lord.
units.m: A blank, my lord.

units.o: She never told her love, / But let concealment, like a worm i’ th’ bud, / Feed on her damask cheek:
units.m: She never told her love, but let concealment, like a worm in the bud, feed on her rosy cheek.

units.o: she pined in thought, / And with a green and yellow melancholy / She sat like patience on a monument, / Smiling at grief.
units.m: She pined away in silent longing, and with a green and yellow melancholy she sat like Patience carved on a monument, smiling at grief.

units.o: Was not this love, indeed?
units.m: Wasn't this love indeed?

units.o: We men may say more, swear more, but indeed, / Our shows are more than will;
units.m: We men may say more, swear more, but in fact our show is greater than what we really feel;

units.o: for still we prove / Much in our vows, but little in our love.
units.m: for we always prove much in our vows, but little in our love.

reasons: Untranslated line fixed: 'Our shows are more than will' = our outward show exceeds our real inclination (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, will: 'disposition, inclination, bent of mind', citing 'our shows are more than w.', Tw. II,4,120). Current 'our shows are more than our will' leaves the line as it was.

Flattened phrase fixed: 'pined in thought' = wasted away in love brooded on in silence (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, thought 1, 'often applied to love, as a passion bred and nourished in the mind', citing 'she pined in t.'; Onions 1911, thought 1 'care, anxiety, sorrow, melancholy'). Current 'She pined in her thoughts' is heard as daydreaming; 'silent longing' carries both the love and the unspoken grief.

Image made clear by ear: 'patience on a monument' = a carved figure of Patience on a tomb (Onions 1911, monument 3 'statue, effigy', 1 'place of burial'). A listener cannot hear the capital P, so 'carved' makes Patience a statue rather than a quality.

Famous lines kept recognizable: 'She never told her love', 'like a worm in the bud', 'green and yellow melancholy', 'smiling at grief'. 'A blank' = an unwritten page (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, blank 1, citing this line); 'damask' = blush-red (Onions 1911, damask, citing 'her d. cheek'), current 'rosy' kept; 'still' = always (Onions 1911), current 'always' kept. 'Was not this' -> 'Wasn't this'.

paragraphs.speaker: DUKE.
paragraphs.proposed: DUKE. But did your sister die of her love, my boy?

units.o: But died thy sister of her love, my boy?
units.m: But did your sister die of her love, my boy?

reasons: keep.

paragraphs.speaker: VIOLA.
paragraphs.proposed: VIOLA. I am all the daughters of my father's house, and all the brothers too. And yet I don't know. Sir, shall I go to this lady?

units.o: I am all the daughters of my father’s house, / And all the brothers too:
units.m: I am all the daughters of my father's house, and all the brothers too.

units.o: and yet I know not.
units.m: And yet I don't know.

units.o: Sir, shall I to this lady?
units.m: Sir, shall I go to this lady?

reasons: Archaic syntax fixed: current keeps the negative 'I know not'. The riddle 'I am all the daughters ... and all the brothers too' is deliberate and stays unexplained (Standard rule 7). The rest of current is kept.

paragraphs.speaker: DUKE.
paragraphs.proposed: DUKE. Yes, that's the business at hand. Go to her quickly. Give her this jewel, and say my love can give no ground and can bear no denial.

units.o: Ay, that’s the theme.
units.m: Yes, that's the business at hand.

units.o: To her in haste.
units.m: Go to her quickly.

units.o: Give her this jewel; say / My love can give no place, bide no denay.
units.m: Give her this jewel, and say my love can give no ground and can bear no denial.

reasons: Ambiguous by ear, fixed: 'theme' = business, matter in hand (Onions 1911, theme 2). Current 'that's the matter' is heard as 'what's the matter' (a problem).
Archaic ellipsis fixed: current keeps 'To her in haste.'

'bide no denay' = cannot endure a denial (Onions 1911, denay sb. 'denial', citing this line). Current 'will tolerate no denial' is accurate but flat; 'will take no denial' is the natural idiom and echoes Orsino's refusal to 'be so answer'd'.

reviewer_fixes.reason: 'can' governs both verbs: inability, not refusal (Schmidt bide 2a).

structure_notes: 9.36 is a parser fragment: the Duke's speech (9.34) is interrupted by the stage direction 9.35 [_Exeunt Curio and Attendants._] and continues in 9.36 with no speaker prefix. Kept without a prefix, as in the current text. In audio a listener gets no cue that the Duke is still speaking; worth fixing at the edition level (restoring 'DUKE.'), not in a content pass.

Cross-paragraph echoes to review together: 9.38 'accept such an answer' / 9.39 'accept that answer'; 9.40 'the love a woman can bear me ... the love I bear Olivia' / 9.43 'what love women may bear to men'.
o_lines follow the TN-A convention: where a sentence ends mid-line (9.39, 9.40, 9.45, 9.47, 9.48), adjacent units share that line number, and each unit's 'o' field quotes the exact original words.
9.41 ends in an interruption ('I know—'); kept as a spaced em dash ('I know —') as in the current text.
Convention: curly apostrophes normalized to straight in all proposed text; no word changes in 'keep' paragraphs.
current_defects: 9.36: mis-gloss: 'common land' for 'dirty lands' (filthy land, said in contempt; Schmidt dirty, Onions dirty).
9.36: non-word and false friend: 'fickly' is not English ('giddily' = carelessly; Schmidt giddily 2); 'parts' (endowments; Schmidt part, Onions part sb. 3) left, heard as body parts.
9.36: metaphors left unexplained: 'queen of jewels which nature decks her in' (her beauty); 'sovereign cruelty' (supreme Cruelty, i.e. Olivia; Schmidt sovereign 2) left abstract.
9.39: meaning shift, echo broken: 'Must she not then be given her answer?' (receive) for 'be answer'd' (accept), losing Viola's turn of Orsino's 'I cannot be so answer'd'.

9.40: false friend left: noun 'revolt' (= revulsion of appetite; Onions revolt sb. 3); 'suffers gluttony' unidiomatic; 'liver' (seat of passion) unexplained; 'what I feel for Olivia' breaks the 'bear me / owe (= bear) Olivia' parallel that Viola answers; intensifier 'all' ('all as hungry as the sea') dropped (minor).
9.43: inverted archaic syntax kept: 'as it might be perhaps, were I a woman, I should love your lordship' ('should' heard as obligation); stray comma in 'Too well, what love'.

9.45: untranslated: 'our shows are more than our will' (will = inclination; Schmidt will); flattened: 'pined in her thoughts' for 'pined in thought' (love brooded on in silence; Schmidt thought 1); archaic 'Was not this'; 'Patience on a monument' ambiguous by ear.
9.47: archaic negative left: 'I know not'.
9.48: ambiguous by ear: 'that's the matter' ('theme' = business in hand; Onions theme 2) is heard as 'what's the matter'; archaic ellipsis 'To her in haste'.
All TN-C paragraphs: convention: curly apostrophes throughout.

reviewer_fixes_applied.find: I'd make myself a willow cabin at your gate — willow, the tree of rejected lovers — and call out to you, my soul, inside the house.
reviewer_fixes_applied.replace: I'd make myself a willow cabin at your gate, like a forsaken lover, and call out to you, my soul, inside the house.
reviewer_fixes_applied.reason: The gloss (willow = emblem of forsaken love: Furness; Onions) was a footnote-style aside in Viola's most famous speech; folded into her own plea. The TN blind reader made the same point.

reviewer_fixes_applied.find: the king sleeps beside a beggar
reviewer_fixes_applied.replace: the king lies by a beggar
reviewer_fixes_applied.reason: 'lies' = lodges, dwells (Schmidt lie vb. 7, citing this line; Malone in Furness), with the lie/lie quibble; 'sleeps beside' narrowed it to a bed image.

reviewer_fixes_applied.find: ever since written bonds disgraced them
reviewer_fixes_applied.reason: A recorded crux: bonds = confinement and money bonds (Deighton), limits and contracts (Chambers) (Furness: 'dark passage'). Plain 'bonds' keeps both senses; 'since' may be temporal or causal.

reviewer_fixes_applied.find: but of the palate, which overeats, grows sick of the taste, and revolts in disgust.
reviewer_fixes_applied.replace: but of the palate — an appetite that is glutted, grows sick of the taste, and revolts in disgust.
reviewer_fixes_applied.reason: Crux 'That suffer surfeit': taken as appetite, after Deighton and Furness (Malone and Innes refer the plural 'suffer' to women). The draft made 'palate' the subject, a reading no Variorum commentator gives; 'overeats' also made 'suffer surfeit' active.

reviewer_fixes_applied.find: if you lead these graces to the grave
reviewer_fixes_applied.replace: if you choose to lead these graces to the grave
reviewer_fixes_applied.reason: 'will' is volitional; Viola's charge of cruelty rests on the choice.

reviewer_fixes_applied.find: I see you for what you are
reviewer_fixes_applied.reason: The original's 'you' is proleptic (Abbott §414); 'see you for what you are' adds a sneer. The current wording was more exact.

reviewer_fixes_applied.replace: My birth is above my present fortunes
reviewer_fixes_applied.reason: The fragment needed its subject; Olivia repeats the line at 5.131, so it must stand alone.

reviewer_fixes_applied.find: that I am loath to reason with them.
reviewer_fixes_applied.replace: that I am loath to use them to prove a reason.
reviewer_fixes_applied.reason: 'prove reason with them' = demonstrate a reason by words (Schmidt prove f); 'reason with them' is heard as persuading someone.
Feste's delayed answer 'My lady is within, sir' (11.26) depends on the word; 'within' is still plain English.
'can' governs both verbs: inability, not refusal (Schmidt bide 2a).
